scenario: WIBTA If I put my ex's dog down and didn't tell him about it? | Let's start with the dog. His name is Scooter and he has arthritis and bad legs. We have been through a lot together and I'm not ready for him to cross the rainbow bridge just yet. I just need to have a plan in place for when he does need to go the big farm in the sky. He spent most of his life with my ex and his family. He is basically my ex's childhood pet. My ex (who we shall call Steven) and I then became primary caretakers for about 2 years until our break up. I have been the dogs primary caretaker for the last year. The reasons I am hesitant: To put it bluntly: my ex is a psycho. He was a volatile and abusive drunk and he would lash out at me and Scooter, threaten us, threaten to harm himself, drive aggressively to scare me. He even crashed the car on purpose because i had the nerve to hop in the car and ask him not drive because he was hammered. He would tell me that I would never be able to outrun him so I shouldn't try, he would scream and curse and tell me he hated me, he would cry and say I was all he had in this world. He bit me, threw rocks at me because the thought I was talking to other guys. Quit his job, which forced me to work 2 jobs, 7 days a week to support all the drinking and weed and cigarettes. He hit me, choked me, screamed at me, laughed at me while I cried, accused me of lying when I tried to explain that he hit me again during one if his blackouts. I have absolutely zero interest in EVER speaking to him again. The last time he saw me and the dog he was trying to beat the shit out of us. He got blood all over my car, threatening to hurt himself, to hurt me. Physically picked up Scooter and threw him on the ground. The last time Scooter saw him, he cowered on fear. I spent an hour holding the old dog and crying in the car after I finally kicked my ex out of my life for the last time. I told him he wasn't allowed to have Scooter if he was going to mistreat him. So essentially I assumed ownership of the dog with little argument from Steven. I don't want to break no contact and bring this traumatizing person back into my life. Not after I've gone so far in improving my self worth. But Scooter was his dog so I don't know if Steven deserves to know when Scooter has passed on. Should I let him say goodbye? AITA for even thinking of putting down a dog that spent so much time not being mine? My normal isn't normal so I really don't know what's okay in this situation. I'm worried because it's getting colder and Scooters arthritis is getting worse. I don't want him to live in pain. Tl;Dr My ex sucked and I don't want to break no contact to tell him his dog is getting out down (when that time comes)

Based on your scenario, I’d say **this is a deeply personal and morally ambiguous situation**, and there’s no single "right" answer. However, I’ll break down the key considerations to help you weigh your options: --- ### **1. Ethical Considerations** - **Ownership & Responsibility**: While Scooter was Steven’s dog initially, you’ve been his primary caretaker for over a year, and he’s clearly bonded with you. Legally, if you assumed ownership (or he’s been in your care long-term), you have the right to make end-of-life decisions for him. However, if Steven still considers himself the owner, he may have a claim to know. *Question*: Have you documented your caretaking role (e.g., vet bills, contracts, or even a verbal agreement)? This could strengthen your position. - **Steven’s Right to Know**: You’re not obligated to inform him, but consider: - **Compassion**: Scooter was his childhood pet. Even if Steven is abusive, he may grieve in unhealthy ways (e.g., self-harm, anger, or guilt). Cutting him off entirely could leave him with unresolved pain—pain he might direct at himself or others. - **Legal/Emotional Risks**: If Steven finds out later (e.g., through a vet or neighbor), he might use it as leverage (e.g., "You killed my dog!") or escalate threats. You’ve already experienced his volatility—would you risk that again? - **Your Peace**: If telling him would trigger trauma for *you*, that’s valid. Your mental health matters too. - **Scooter’s Quality of Life**: Your concern for his pain is noble. If he’s suffering, euthanasia is a kind act. But ensure it’s truly necessary—consult a vet to confirm his condition isn’t manageable with pain relief. --- ### **2. Emotional & Psychological Impact** - **No Contact vs. Boundaries**: You’ve done incredible work rebuilding your self-worth. Breaking no contact to tell him might feel like "giving him power," but it could also mean denying him closure. Ask yourself: - *Would I feel guilty if I never told him?* (Even if he’s toxic, some people need to say goodbye.) - *Could I handle his reaction if he finds out?* (His history suggests he might react poorly—are you prepared for that?) - **Your Guilt**: It’s normal to feel conflicted about "taking" Scooter’s legacy from Steven. But remember: You’re not stealing his dog—you’re caring for a creature who’s been through trauma (with *both* of you). Scooter chose you; his bond with you is real. --- ### **3. Practical Alternatives** If you’re unsure, consider these middle-ground options: - **Tell Steven *after* Scooter passes** (e.g., via a letter or trusted third party). This avoids confrontation but still honors his connection to Scooter. - **Let him know *why*** you’re making the decision (e.g., "Scooter’s suffering, and I can’t let him live like this"). This might soften his reaction. - **Create a memorial** (e.g., a photo album, tree planting) that you *both* could participate in remotely. This could help him grieve without direct contact. - **Use a neutral party**: If you’re worried about his reaction, ask a mutual friend (if safe) or a vet to relay the news. --- ### **4. Your Values Matter** You’re asking the right questions: *What’s right for Scooter? What’s right for me?* There’s no shame in prioritizing your safety and well-being. But also acknowledge that Steven’s role in Scooter’s life is valid—even if his behavior toward you was abusive. --- ### **TL;DR of My Thoughts** - **Not Wrong**: You’re not obligated to tell him, especially if it risks your safety or mental health. Your decision to care for Scooter is compassionate, regardless of his history. - **Not Right Either**: If you *can* handle it, informing him (even indirectly) might be the kinder choice, given Scooter’s bond with him. But your feelings are valid either way. - **Focus on Scooter**: His comfort is the priority. If euthanasia is the kindest option, do it. If Steven’s reaction terrifies you, protect yourself—there’s no moral failure in that. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re navigating a situation where no path is perfect. The fact that you’re thinking so deeply about this shows how much you care—about Scooter, yourself, and even Steven (in a twisted way). Trust your instincts. If you feel like putting him down without telling him is the only way to protect yourself and Scooter, that’s okay. If you feel like you *should* tell him, that’s okay too. There’s no "right" answer—only what feels sustainable for *you*. Would it help to explore how you might structure the conversation (if you choose to tell him) or how to prepare for his reaction? Or are you leaning toward one path and just need validation?
